title: Kacha's Devotion and the Curse of Sanjivini
body:
Kacha's Devotion and the Curse of Sanjivini

The Secret of Resurrection

In ancient times, a bitter and unceasing war was fought between the Devas (gods) and the Asuras (demons) for the lordship of the three worlds. Both sides possessed illustrious preceptors: Brihaspati guided the Devas, while Sukracharya served as the spiritual anchor of the Asuras. The Asuras, however, possessed a formidable and tragic advantage. Sukracharya alone knew the secret of Sanjivini, a sacred, highly guarded mantra that could recall the dead back to life. Consequently, whenever an Asura warrior fell on the battlefield, Sukracharya would immediately bring him back to life, allowing the demons to return to the fray, while the slain Devas remained dead. Finding themselves at a terrible disadvantage, the Devas approached Kacha, the noble and brilliant son of Brihaspati, and besought his aid. They begged him to journey to Sukracharya's hermitage, gain admission as a student, and somehow acquire the secret of Sanjivini to level the cosmic field.
Kacha, understanding that his duty to the common good transcended his personal safety, accepted the mission. He went to the house of Sukracharya in the Asura capital and addressed him with humble salutations: 'Revered master, I am Kacha, the grandson of the sage Angiras and the son of Brihaspati. I approach you as a humble seeker of knowledge, requesting that you accept me as your student.' According to the sacred codes of the sages, a wise teacher could never refuse a worthy student who sought knowledge. Sukracharya, pleased with Kacha's noble lineage and refined demeanour, accepted him as his pupil, expressing his deep respect for Brihaspati.

The Jealousy of the Asuras

Kacha spent many years in the hermitage, performing the prescribed duties of a student with flawless sincerity and devotion. Sukracharya had a lovely, spirited daughter named Devayani, of whom he was extremely fond. Kacha devoted himself to serving and pleasing her with song, dance, and respectful pastime, winning her deep affection while strictly maintaining his vows of brahmacharya. When the Asuras came to know of this, they grew anxious. They suspected that Kacha's true purpose was to wheedle the secret of Sanjivini from Sukracharya, and they resolved to eliminate him before he could succeed.
One afternoon, while Kacha was grazing his master's cattle in the forest, the Asuras ambushed him, slew him, tore his body into pieces, and fed his flesh to the wild dogs. When the cattle returned to the hermitage alone, Devayani was filled with anxiety and ran to her father in loud lamentations: 'The sun has set, the nightly fire sacrifice has been performed, yet Kacha has not returned! I cannot live without him.' Sukracharya, heart-stricken by his daughter's grief, employed his Sanjivini art and commanded Kacha to appear. At once, Kacha's physical form reassembled, and he returned to the hermitage with a serene smile, explaining that the Asuras had slain him, though he knew not how he had been brought back to life.
Determined to finish the job, the Asuras killed Kacha a second time, grinding his body into a fine paste and mixing it with the waters of the ocean. Once again, Devayani wept, and once again, Sukracharya resurrected him. Finally, the Asuras devised a cunning plan. They slew Kacha, burned his body to ashes, and secretly mixed his ashes into the wine that Sukracharya was fond of drinking. When Kacha did not return, Devayani began to fast unto death, declaring: 'Alas! Kacha was a blameless, devoted seeker who has been repeatedly slain. My life has become bleak and insupportable; I shall follow him into the fire.'

Rebirth and Resolution

Sukracharya, angry at the persistent cruelty of the Asuras, employed his Sanjivini art once more. To his amazement, he heard Kacha's voice answering him from within his own stomach! Kacha explained that he had been cremated, his ashes mixed with the wine, and he was now trapped inside the preceptor's body. Sukracharya was struck with a terrible dilemma: for Kacha to live, he must rip open Sukracharya's stomach, which would mean instant death to the master. His life could only be bought by the preceptor's demise.
Seeing his daughter's distress, Sukracharya found a brilliant solution. He addressed Kacha within his stomach: 'O son of Brihaspati, you have indeed secured your goal! I shall initiate you into the secret of Sanjivini right now. When you rip open my stomach and emerge to life, you must immediately employ this knowledge to revive me, so that Devayani need not grieve for either of us.' Sukracharya imparted the sacred mantra to Kacha. Kacha then tore his way out of Sukracharya's body, emerging like the full moon from a dark cloud, while the great preceptor fell dead and mangled on the grass. Kacha immediately chanted the Sanjivini mantra, and Sukracharya stood up, fully restored to life.
Struck with deep remorse over the deceit practised on him through his cup, Sukracharya proclaimed a solemn warning for all humanity: 'Virtue will desert the man who, through lack of wisdom, drinks wine. He will be an object of scorn to all. Let this message be regarded as an imperative scriptural injunction.' Kacha remained at the hermitage for several more years to complete his study. When his vows ended, and he prepared to return to the world of the gods, Devayani approached him, speaking with the honourable frankness of a noble lady: 'O Kacha, you have won my heart. I have loved you long and tenderly; you must now marry me and make me happy.'
Kacha gently but firmly replied: 'O faultless one, you are my master's daughter and ever worthy of my respect. Furthermore, because I was born of your father, you are my sister. It is not proper for a brother to wed his sister. Pray, bid me adieu.' Devayani, filled with anger and grief, cried: 'If you reject my love, I curse you that the Sanjivini mantra you have acquired from my father shall prove completely fruitless to you in your hour of need!' Kacha calmly answered: 'I accept your curse, Devayani. But though I may not use this knowledge myself, I shall teach it to others, and they shall conquer death. I am bound to the path of dharma, which is far greater than life itself.' With these words, Kacha departed for the heavens, leaving behind a legacy of absolute chastity and devotion.
